name: Dartfish
tagline: Video tagging, telestration and side-by-side comparison software used by coaches and sports scientists.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Dartfish sells several tiers plus team and institutional licensing, so a single monthly number would be fiction.

verdictSummary: The parts people use most days are a tagging panel, a timeline, slow motion, drawing on frames and two clips playing side by side. All of that is a weekend of browser video work plus ffmpeg, and for one coach with one camera it genuinely holds up. What does not come free is the boring professional plumbing: live capture with delayed playback on the touchline, multi-camera sync, frame-accurate stepping across codecs, mobile capture, and a sharing model that a whole squad can actually use. Dartfish also sits inside federation and university workflows where the file formats and the reporting are expected to look a certain way. So: a real personal tool, not a replacement for a department's install.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that loads your match video, lets you tag events with single keypresses into a searchable timeline, draw angles and lines on a paused frame, compare two clips in sync, and export tagged clips with ffmpeg.
requirements: Node 20 and a modern Chromium browser
Source video transcoded to H.264 mp4 for reliable seeking
Local disk space for clip exports
A machine that can scrub 1080p or 4K without crying
whatYouLose: Live capture with instant delayed replay during a session
Multi-camera and multi-angle sync on one timeline
Frame-accurate stepping and genuinely smooth variable-speed playback across arbitrary codecs
Mobile capture and tagging on a phone or tablet at the pitch
Team and athlete sharing, plus the reports and export formats institutions expect
moatNotes: The moat is less software than workflow: coaching staff trained on it, federations expecting its outputs, and years of tuning for the specific pain of scrubbing sports footage.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the value is measured in minutes saved during a 48 hour turnaround between matches, not in features on a list. Dartfish has had two decades to sand down everything that goes wrong with real sports footage: odd frame rates, long files, multiple cameras, cheap handhelds, tagging while the game is still happening. A personal build covers the happy path and then breaks the first time you hand it a 4K 50fps file from a club camera and ask for frame-by-frame on a knee angle. Teams also pay for the fact that the assistant coach already knows which key does what.
notes: Great self-build if you are one person analysing your own footage; bad idea if an entire squad depends on it by Tuesday.
prompt:
Build a local-first sports video analysis tool. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry. Everything runs on my machine against local video files.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript front end
- Small Express server in the same repo for file access and clip export
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for projects, tags and drawings
- ffmpeg and ffprobe invoked as child processes for probing and clip export
- Plain CSS, no UI framework

Features that must work:
1. Point the app at a local folder; list video files found there with duration and frame rate from ffprobe.
2. Player view: HTML5 video, keyboard scrubbing (arrow keys step by one frame using frame rate, shift for ten frames), playback speeds 0.1x to 2x, loop a selected in/out range.
3. Tagging panel: user-defined event categories with single-key bindings, stored per project. Pressing a key records an event at the current time with a configurable lead-in and lead-out, for example 5s before and 3s after.
4. Timeline below the player showing all tagged events as colored blocks, clickable to jump, draggable at edges to trim.
5. Event list with filters by category, free text note per event, delete and edit.
6. Drawing: pause and draw lines, arrows, circles and an angle measurement tool on a canvas overlay. Save drawings attached to that timestamp, redraw them when returning to it.
7. Compare view: two players side by side, each loaded with any event clip, with a linked scrub and a frame offset slider so I can align two different attempts.
8. Export: for selected events, call ffmpeg to cut clips with stream copy where possible, re-encoding only when the cut point demands it. Also export the event list as CSV.

Out of scope, do not build: live camera capture, multi-camera sync, user auth, any mobile app, any hosted deployment.

Deliverables: working repo, npm run dev starts server and front end together, README with ffmpeg install notes and a short keyboard shortcut table. Put any config such as the media root in .env with an .env.example committed. Seed the database with one sample tag set for football so the tagging panel is not empty on first run.
